results.content: Metadata schema — European Language Grid 1 documentation Chapter 3: Contributing to ELG * Contribute a lexical/conceptual resource * Update / Delete a catalogue entry * Contribute via an external repository * Validating items contributed to ELG * Validate a functional LT service (at technical/metadata level) * Validate an LRT hosted in ELG (at technical/metadata level) * Validate a functional LT service or ELG hosted LRT at legal level * Validate a “metadata record only” (at metadata level) * Minimal elements for all entities * Minimal elements for all language resources and technologies * Minimal elements for tools/services * Minimal elements for language descriptions * Minimal elements for lexical/conceptual resources * Internal LT Service API specification Annex 3: Processes and policies Annex 4: Publications and reports Develop and launch modern apps with MongoDB Atlas, a resilient data platform. A Language Resource can be described through a set of metadata elements common to all, and a further set that fits to each of these four types. You can find the full schema XSD, documentation as well as templates and examples of metadata records for all resource types in the ELG SHARE schema Git repository. You can browse the full schema documentation here: The minimal version comprises a set of carefully selected metadata elements that are deemed important for various reasons, such as: * _identification and citation_: resource name(s); identifier(s); a short description of contents; versioning information; a contact point for further information (email or landing page); data of the resource provider(s) and resource creator(s); classification by domain, keywords and intended LT application; language coverage (language and, if needed, dialect); publication date; * _support_: links to manuals, training material; samples of the resource; * _usage/access_: distribution form (e.g. as downloadable file, a form that can be accessed via an interface, source code or binary file of software, etc.); licensing conditions; access location. Additional metadata elements, particular to each resource type, are required, such as size and format for data files, prerequisites for tools and services, etc.

results.title: JSON Schema
results.content: # JSON Schema. JSON Schema is a grammar language for defining the structure, content, and (to some extent) semantics of JSON objects. It lets you specify metadata (data about data) about what an object’s properties mean and what values are valid for those properties. It’s often necessary for applications to validate JSON objects, to ensure that required properties are present and that additional validation constraints (such as a price never being less than one dollar) are met. These validations are typically performed in the context of *JSON Schema*. When we validate a JSON document without its Schema, we are validating only the syntax of the document. Syntactic validation guarantees only that the document is well-formed. The tools such as JSONLint, and the JSON parsers perform only Syntactic validations. Semantic validation is more than syntactic validation. It performs the syntax checks as well as the data checks. Semantic validation helps in ensuring that the client is sending only allowed fields in JSON documents and not any invalid name-value pairs. JSON Schema is a grammar language for defining the structure, content, and (to some extent) semantics of JSON objects. It lets you specify metadata (data about data) about what an object’s properties mean and what values are valid for those properties. The result of applying the grammar language to a JSON document is the schema (a blueprint) describing the set of JSON objects that are valid according to the schema. 1. JSON Schema is itself a JSON object. 2. JSON Schema grammer is maintained at. 3. It describes the existing data format. 5. It provides complete structural validation, which is useful for automated testing and validating client-submitted data. Let’s consider the following JSN schema :. { "$schema": "", "title": "Person", "description": "A person", "type": "object", "properties": { "name": { "description": "A person's name", "type": "string" }, "age": { "description": "A person's age", "type": "number", "minimum": 18, "maximum": 64 } }, "required": ["name", "age"] }. The JSON Schema website provides links to various validator implementations for different programming languages (see ). We have used the online validator at JSONSchemaLint in the given example. Invalid JSON document example (age > 64). ### JSON with JSONPath.

This project provides the JSON schemas for defining metadata fields and their requirements for The National Archives. This project provides a set of JSON schemas that define the structure and requirements of metadata fields used in TNA Digital Archiving. The schema are designed to conform to the JSON Schema specification, extended to include custom keywords and properties specific to TNA Digital Archiving metadata requirements. ## JSON Schema. ## Schemas. ### Validation schemas used to define the metadata. These schemas are used by the JSON schema validator to validate metadata. #### Additional schemas are used to define specific use cases for metadata. The base schema defines the metadata fields that are supported within Digital Archiving. #### Required Schema. The required schema defines the required fields in a metadata file uploaded to TDR. The data load SharePoint schema defines what properties are permitted when loading metadata directly from SharePoint. ### Error file schema. The output of a metadata file validation should be a JSON file conforming to the error file schema. An example of an error file conforming to this schema.
